feed.title: Field Notes
feed.subtitle: An amateur investigation, with corrections. Built with SiteSquatch.

entry.title: Honey, I Shrunk the Site
entry.summary: What the build weighs, and a picture that got lighter on the way out.
entry.content:
The beaver weighs her pack before every hike, so she asked what this site weighs. After ssqch build:

ssqch footprint

It lists the build by kind of file (pages, images, CSS, feeds), then the heaviest pages and files. Most of this site's weight is one picture: the stump, from the second entry.

The camera's copy, src/img/stump.jpg, is 47.9 KB. The build makes six copies of it, three widths in WebP and JPEG, 107 KB together, and the footprint weighs every one. A reader carries only one: the browser picks the width its screen needs, in WebP when it can read it. On a phone or a laptop's sharp screen that's the widest WebP, 14.7 KB, under a third of the camera's copy. The JPEG copies are for browsers that can't read WebP.

To hear about it when something gets heavy, give each kind of file a budget in ssqch.config.js:

budgets: { pages: "50 KB", images: "40 KB" },

A file over its kind's budget is a warning after every build, saying which file and by how much:

warn: /img/jsuIfm9F_f-1200.jpeg (42.3 KB) is over the images budget of 40.0 KB

ssqch footprint dist-before weighs another build, to compare before and after a change, and --format json gives the same numbers to a script or an agent.

The beaver's pack came in under budget. She would like that noted.

entry.title: The Stump Has a Forwarding Address
entry.summary: A post that moved, and the old address that still gets you here.
entry.content:
This entry used to be at /posts/where-did-the-stump-go/. I renamed it, because the stump didn't go anywhere: it has a forwarding address. A ranger had already pinned the old link to the station's notice board, and it still works. Try it: the old address.

A post's address comes from its file name, so renaming the file moves the post. The old address goes in the post's front matter:

aliases: [/posts/where-did-the-stump-go/]

redirectsPlugin() in ssqch.config.js gives each old address a small page that sends readers, and search engines, on to the new one. An old address that's another page's address stops the build, so a redirect never hides a post.

On Netlify or Cloudflare, redirectsPlugin({ hostFile: true }) writes each one to _redirects instead, and the host answers with a real 301.

The tracks lead back to the stump. They always do.

entry.title: The Cache of the Wild
entry.summary: A raccoon, the trail conditions, and a copy for when the network is down.
entry.content:
The raccoon keeps a dated copy of the trail conditions. He checks the ranger station once a day, and the rest of the time he reads you his copy. When the station doesn't answer, he reads you his copy anyway and mentions how old it is.

A data file that asks a server for something can do the same. Save this as src/_data/conditions.js, and every page has conditions:

export default async function () {
  // Asked once a day; until then, the saved copy in .cache/ssqch/fetch/.
  const response = await fetch("https://api.example.com/trails/cedar", { cache: "1d" });
  return response.json();
}
  • While ssqch serve rebuilds on every save, the server is asked once a day, not once a save.
  • When the server is down and there's a copy, the build uses it and says how old it is.
  • ssqch build --offline uses only the saved copies, whatever their age, so a build on a plane never touches the network.

The raccoon has never been on a plane. He has opinions about the Old Growth trail.

entry.title: Raiders of the Lost Path
entry.summary: An old map, a renamed heading, and the build that caught it.
entry.content:
A ranger came by with an old map of these notes. It pointed to a heading called "The tracks". I had renamed it "Where they lead" the week before. The ranger was not pleased, and neither was the build.

What the build said

The link checker (linksPlugin() in ssqch.config.js) follows every link inside the site after a production build. A link to a page that isn't there, or to a heading that isn't on it, fails the build and says where:

error: after_build hook failed: linksPlugin: the trail goes cold on 1 broken link:
  /posts/i-know-what-i-saw/ -> /posts/the-stump-has-moved/#the-tracks (no id "the-tracks" on that page)

The correction

A heading's id comes from its text, so renaming a heading moves its address. Point the link at the new one, #where-they-lead, or keep the old heading. In ssqch serve it's a warning, so you can keep writing while you look for it.

This link works, for comparison: back to what the build said.

entry.title: The Stump Has Moved
entry.content:
I went back a third time. The stump is gone. There are tracks.

More as it develops. To start an entry of your own:

ssqch new posts --title "My second sighting"

It copies src/_blueprints/posts.md and fills in the title and today's date. Add draft: true to a post's front matter to keep it out of production builds until you're sure of what you saw.

entry.title: Upon Further Review, a Stump
entry.summary: A correction to the previous entry.
entry.content:
I went back in daylight. It was a stump. A tall one, to be fair to me.

The description in this post's front matter is the page's meta description; posts without one get the site's, from src/_data/site.json.

I did get a picture this time. It's a little blurry, but you can clearly see the stump.

The picture is src/img/stump.jpg, and this post shows it with ![A blurry photo...](/img/stump.jpg). The build turns it into a <picture> in three sizes, so it stays sharp on any screen. Whether it was sharp to begin with is between you and your camera.

A raccoon who keeps everything told me the trick for deploying: keep dist/img/ and .cache/ between builds, and the build never encodes the same picture twice. Raccoon's cache. Raccoon did not see anything tall.

entry.title: I Know What I Saw
entry.content:
It was tall, it was in a hurry, and it was gone before I found my camera. I'm writing it down anyway. This is the first entry in my field notes.

It's also your first post. Every Markdown file in src/posts/ is a post: posts.json gives them all the layout and the posts tag, so they show up on the home page, newest first. The tags in a post's front matter add it to a page for each tag (this one's on sightings), and every post is in the feed, /feed.xml (feedPlugin() in ssqch.config.js).

Edit this file while ssqch serve is running, and the page reloads by itself.
